title: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans
subtitle: truly born, truly nailed, truly raised: a prisoner's letter against a Christ who only seemed
lead: From Troas, on his way to die in Rome, Ignatius of Antioch writes back to the church at Smyrna, where he had stayed. Some teachers there said Christ 'suffered only in appearance' (2:1). Ignatius answers with a string of facts, each stamped 'truly': Christ was truly of David's family, truly born of a virgin, truly nailed under Pontius Pilate and Herod, truly raised, and in the flesh after the resurrection, when he said, 'Take hold, feel me and see that I am not a bodiless demon' (1:1-3:2).

The second half holds the lines churches have argued over most in Ignatius: the thanksgiving that 'is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ' (7:1), the 'valid' thanksgiving 'under the overseer' (8:1), and 'wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the catholic church' (8:2), which the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Missouri Synod call the first use of the phrase. No church counts the letter as Scripture; it is read here as an early witness, with the New Testament as the measure.
facts: No church. It is not in the New Testament of the Council of Trent (Catholic), the Westminster Confession (Reformed), the Second London Baptist Confession, the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church's list of 35 New Testament books, or the Thirty-Nine Articles' 'Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'.

Ignatius, overseer of the church at Antioch in Syria, on his way to execution in Rome. Eusebius names the letter and quotes 3:1-2 (Church History 3.36.10-11); Jerome quotes it too (Lives of Illustrious Men 16).

Written at Troas (12:1), after the letters from Smyrna, one of which, To the Romans, is dated 24 August (Lake). Eusebius's Chronicle puts the martyrdom 'in the tenth year of Trajan, i.e. 108 A.D.' (as Lake reports it); Jerome, the eleventh year. Lake: 'a general tendency to think that Ignatius was really a martyr in Rome in the time of Trajan (98-117 A.D.)'.
Troas, on the coast of Asia, by the hand of Burrhus (12:1)
The church at Smyrna in Asia, with its overseer, council of elders and deacons (12:2)
Letter of a condemned prisoner, against false teaching

Kirsopp Lake's Greek (Loeb, 1912), the short (middle) recension: the Medicean manuscript at Florence (G), the long recension (g), the Latin (L), Armenian (A) and Syriac (S) versions, a Sahidic fragment (C), and the Berlin papyrus of the 400s (B), which covers 3:3-12:1.
authorship: The letter claims to be by 'Ignatius, also called Theophorus', a prisoner from Antioch (1:0; 4:1; 11:1). Eusebius knew it among the seven letters and quotes it (Church History 3.36.10-11). A fifth-century papyrus holds most of it (Lake).

The seven letters survive in three forms: a long recension of thirteen letters with interpolations, the short recension of the seven Eusebius names, and a Syriac abridgment of three that does not include Smyrnaeans (Lake). The Catholic Encyclopedia describes the long controversy over their genuineness. In 1910 the Catholic Encyclopedia wrote: 'While it can hardly be said that there is at present any unanimous agreement on the subject, the best modern criticism favors the authenticity of the seven letters mentioned by Eusebius', naming Zahn, Lightfoot and Harnack. Later in the twentieth century the question was opened again. Sergio Zañartu's survey of the recent discussion (Teología y Vida, 2009) names R. Weijenborg (1969), who argued that the short recension was made from the long one; R. Joly (1979), who held the letters a forgery written in Smyrna between 165 and 168; J. Rius-Camps (1980), who kept as genuine only the four letters written from Smyrna; R. M. Hübner (1997), who dated the letters between 165 and 175; and his student T. Lechner (1999). Zañartu quotes W. R. Schoedel (1987), who expected the short recension to remain what 'the scholarly consensus today' sees in it, 'a collection of genuine letters of Bishop Ignatius of Antioch', and C. Munier's survey of a century of research (1993), which found no reason in 'the general opinion of historians and patrologists' to give up the conclusions of the nineteenth-century scholars. Zañartu himself, after weighing the objections, holds to the short recension's authenticity 'until the contrary is proved' (the quotations from his survey are the site's translations). On the other side, B. A. Zuiddam (Ekklesiastikos Pharos, 2010) argues that the seven-letter text may be a medieval abridgment, and that either the whole collection is 'a pious fraud to strengthen orthodoxy of a later date' or eleven letters are Ignatius's own. Lake follows the short recension.

audience.to: The church at Smyrna, a port of the Roman province of Asia, where Ignatius had stayed on the way to Rome. It had an overseer (unnamed in this letter; the companion letter To Polycarp is addressed to 'Polycarp, overseer of the church of the Smyrnaeans'), a council of elders and deacons (12:2), households with wives and children and a group of 'widows' (13:1), and it had sent Burrhus with Ignatius as his helper (12:1). Some in or near the church followed teachers who said Christ suffered 'only in appearance' and who kept away from the church's thanksgiving and prayer (2:1; 7:1).
audience.why: To strengthen a church Ignatius loved against those teachers: by confirming the faith it held (1:1-3:3), by warning it to keep away from them but pray for them (4:1-7:2), by binding it to its overseer so that no separate meal or baptism could pass as the church's (8:1-9:1), and by asking it to send an envoy to Antioch, now at peace (11:1-3). Knowing that a rival meal existed explains why the letter's sharpest words about the Supper and the bishop stand side by side.
views: Lake describes them as holding 'docetism (δοκεῖν), which regarded the sufferings, and in some cases the life, of Jesus as merely an appearance', and says 'it is disputed' whether the Judaizing tendency of the letters To the Magnesians and To the Philadelphians belonged to the same circles. The Catholic Encyclopedia says that in Ignatius's day 'Docetism seems to have been closely connected with Judaism'.

outline: Greeting to the church in Smyrna
The faith of the Smyrnaeans: truly born, truly nailed
He truly suffered, not 'only in appearance'
In the flesh after the resurrection
Beasts in human form; near the sword is near God
Faith and love are everything; they do not care for the poor
They keep away from the thanksgiving
Follow the overseer; the catholic church
Send an envoy of God to Antioch
Greetings from Troas; the households and the widows

lenses.name: Historical-critical
lenses.desc: Reads the letter as a source: who the opponents were, the witnesses (the Berlin papyrus and the Sahidic fragment beside the medieval copies), the journey from Smyrna to Troas, and the peace at Antioch.

lenses.name: New Testament
lenses.desc: Follows the New Testament in the letter: Luke 24:39 and Acts 10:41 beside the risen Christ of chapter 3, Matthew 3:15 and Romans 1:3 in the confession of 1:1, Matthew 19:12, and 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7 on Christ 'come in the flesh'.

lenses.name: Church order and the churches
lenses.desc: Reads the letter for the questions churches still ask of it: the overseer, the council of elders and the deacons (8:1), the 'valid' thanksgiving and who may lead it (8:1-2), baptism and the love feast, 'the catholic church' (8:2), and the thanksgiving as Christ's flesh (7:1).

sections.h: From Troas, to a church he had stayed with
sections.b: Ignatius wrote to Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles and Rome from Smyrna, and then, at Troas, to Philadelphia, to Smyrna and to Polycarp (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5-10). This letter thanks the Smyrnaeans for refreshing him and his companions (9:2; 10:1), sends greetings from Troas by Burrhus (12:1), and passes on news that the church at Antioch is at peace (11:2).

Chapters 1-7 answer those who said Christ 'suffered only in appearance' (2:1). Ignatius's method is to list facts and repeat 'truly'. He adds the argument from his own chains: 'if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance, then I too am in chains only in appearance' (4:2). He tests the teachers by their deeds: they do not care for the widow, the orphan, the prisoner or the hungry (6:2), and they keep away from the church's thanksgiving, 'because they do not confess that the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior' (7:1). On the teaching see the topic Docetism; on the belief it denies, The Incarnation.

sections.h: The Berlin papyrus and the Sahidic fragment
sections.b: Most witnesses to Ignatius are medieval. For this letter two are much older. A Sahidic (Coptic) fragment 'containing part of the epistle to the Smyrnaeans, from MS. Borg. 248 in the Museo Nazionale at Naples' was published in 1883 and by Lightfoot in 1885; and 'in 1910 a papyrus fragment of the 5th century (Berlin P. 10581) was published by C. Schmidt and W. Schubert ...; this contains Smyrnaeans iii. 3-xii. 1' (Lake). Lake calls all the Greek manuscripts mixed with the long recension 'with the possible exception of the Berlin papyrus'. He often follows the papyrus (5:2; 7:2; 8:2; 9:2; 10:1-2; 11:2-3), but not always (4:2, 'only in appearance'; 10:1, 'Rheus'; 11:3). See the variants.

sections.h: The thanksgiving, the overseer and the catholic church
sections.b: Chapters 7-8 are the part of the letter the churches cite. Catholic teaching quotes 8:1 for the bishop's responsibility for the Eucharist (Catechism 1369) and 8:2 for the meaning of 'catholic' (Catechism 830); the Catholic Encyclopedia counts 7 among the clearest early witnesses to the Real Presence. The Lutheran Church—Missouri Synod's commemoration says Ignatius stressed 'the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper' and was 'the first to use the word catholic'. Lightfoot reads 7:1 as an argument about the reality of Christ's flesh and 8:1 as aimed at a separate meal. Calvin called the writings 'published under the name of Ignatius' 'absurdities' (Institutes 1.13.29); he wrote before Ussher's edition of 1644, and until then, Lake says, 'only the long recension was known'. The card at chapter 8 sets out who may lead the Supper and baptize in the churches today; the views notes at 7:1, 8:1 and 8:2 give the other readings.

Philo, a deacon from Cilicia, and Rheus Agathopus had followed Ignatius from Syria (10:1; To the Philadelphians 11). Burrhus, an Ephesian deacon, carried or wrote the letter (12:1; Ignatius to the Ephesians 2:1). Ignatius greets the overseer, the council of elders and the deacons (12:2), the households, 'the virgins who are called widows' (13:1), the household of Tavia, Alce, Daphnus and Eutecnus (13:2). Lightfoot thought Alce might be the Alce whose brother Nicetes opposed the Christians at Polycarp's death (Martyrdom of Polycarp 17:2).

spec.title: Claude's theory: the meal and the poor belong together
spec.body: Ignatius puts two charges side by side: the teachers 'do not care about love' for the widow, the orphan and the hungry (6:2), and they 'keep away from the thanksgiving' (7:1). If, as Lightfoot thinks, the thanksgiving was still part of a shared meal, the love feast of 8:2, then the church's meal was also where the poor were fed. On that reading the two charges are one: staying away from the church's table meant staying away from its widows and orphans too. This is my suggestion, built on Lightfoot's view of the agape; Ignatius does not draw the link.

prompts: Take hold, feel me and see (3:2)

In a dim upper room lit by one oil lamp, a risen man with wounded hands holds out his arm while a fisherman reaches to touch it; other disciples lean in, one holding a piece of grilled fish; their shadows fall on the wall like cave-painting figures.

Style: sketched by hand onto an old rolled parchment scroll. Sepia and iron-gall ink linework with charcoal shading, red-ochre and yellow-ochre pigment like Lascaux cave paintings, Egyptian hieroglyphic register lines and small glyph borders, plus a few bold flat shapes of lapis blue in the manner of modern paper cut-outs. Visible parchment grain, uneven hand-drawn lines, soft torn irregular edges that fade into the parchment. No frame, no rectangular border, no sharp corners, no lettering. Wide horizontal composition, 3:2.

canon.summary: Ignatius to the Smyrnaeans is an early Christian letter in no church's Bible. Its author, the martyr Ignatius of Antioch, is honored as a saint by Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, and Catholic teaching quotes this letter on the Eucharist and on the word 'catholic'.
accepted_by: Not Scripture: the Council of Trent's list of New Testament books (1546) does not include it. The U.S. bishops' calendar keeps 17 October as the Memorial of 'Saint Ignatius of Antioch, Bishop and Martyr'. The Catechism quotes this letter at 830 and 1369.

Not part of the Bible: Reid (1908) states that the Eastern Orthodox churches 'have a New Testament identical with the Catholic'. The Orthodox Church in America commemorates 'Hieromartyr Ignatius the God-Bearer, Bishop of Antioch' on 20 December.
Not Scripture: the church's list of 35 New Testament books, which adds eight books to the 27, among them 'The book of Clement' and the 'Didascalia', does not name it.

Not Scripture: Article VI receives 'All the Books of the New Testament, as they are commonly received'. The Church of England's Common Worship calendar keeps 17 October as a Lesser Festival of 'Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, Martyr, c.107'.

Commemorates 'Ignatius of Antioch, Pastor and Martyr' on 17 October, and says he stressed 'the reality of Christ's bodily presence in the Lord's Supper' and 'was the first to use the word catholic to describe the universality of the Church'.
Not Scripture: the Westminster Confession lists the 27 books of the New Testament as 'all the books of the Old and New Testaments, which are these'.
Not Scripture: the Second London Baptist Confession (1689) lists the same 27 books, 'All of which are given by the inspiration of God, to be the rule of faith and life'.

provenance.b: Ignatius wrote from Troas (12:1), after leaving Smyrna, where he had written four letters (Eusebius, Church History 3.36.5-10). Burrhus, a deacon of Ephesus whom the Smyrnaeans and Ephesians had sent with him, carried or wrote it (12:1).

In the Greek Medicean manuscript at Florence (G) with the other short-recension letters except Romans, in the long recension, in Latin, Armenian and Syriac versions, in a Sahidic fragment from Naples, and, for 3:3-12:1, in a fifth-century papyrus at Berlin (Lake). Eusebius quotes 3:1-2 (Church History 3.36.11).

rejected_why.h: A bishop's letter, not an apostle's
rejected_why.b: The early church received into the New Testament writings it held to come from the apostles and their circle. Ignatius writes as 'the last' of his church, worthy 'from the grace of God' (11:1), and in his letter to the Romans sets himself below the apostles: 'They were apostles; I am a condemned man' (Ignatius to the Romans 4:3).

rejected_why.h: Treated as a letter of a church writer
rejected_why.b: Eusebius quotes the letter in his history (Church History 3.36.11) and does not mention Ignatius in his survey of the books accepted, disputed and rejected for the New Testament (Church History 3.25). Jerome lists the seven letters in his lives of church writers (Lives of Illustrious Men 16).

cited_in.b: The risen Jesus invites the disciples to touch him. Ignatius's saying, 'Take hold, feel me and see that I am not a bodiless demon', is close in sense but not in words; Lightfoot judges Ignatius's form later than Luke's. The New Testament does not quote this letter.
John's test, confessing 'Jesus Christ as having come in the flesh', is the test Ignatius applies; he calls the deniers' Christ not 'flesh-bearing'.
The reason for Jesus's baptism, 'to fulfill all righteousness', is given only in Matthew; Ignatius has it in his own words (Lake's margin; Lightfoot).
Jude's 'love feasts' (Jude 1:12) and Ignatius's 'love feast' (8:2) both use agapē for a church meal; Lake's footnote at 8:2 points to the same verse of Jude.

reliability.verdict: This is Claude's analysis, not a church's judgment. As a witness to Christian belief and church life early in the second century the letter is of the first importance: it gives a detailed confession of Christ's birth, death and resurrection, the earliest known use of 'the catholic church' (as the Catholic Encyclopedia and the Missouri Synod both say), an overseer with elders and deacons in one city, and a church meal called both thanksgiving and love feast. Besides the usual witnesses, its text has a fifth-century papyrus for most of the letter. Its historical claims are few and fit Eusebius. In doctrine it follows the New Testament closely on Christ; its rules on the overseer go beyond anything the New Testament says.

sections.h: 1. As a witness to early Christian belief
sections.b: High. The letter shows a church in Asia confessing Christ 'truly' born, crucified and raised against teachers who denied his flesh (1:1-3:3), reading the prophets and 'the gospel' (7:2), keeping a meal called the thanksgiving (7:1; 8:1) and the love feast (8:2), and ordered under one overseer with elders and deacons (8:1; 12:2). It also shows a group of 'widows' (13:1) and a household named after a woman, Tavia (13:2).

Good. Besides the medieval Greek copy and the versions, the Berlin papyrus of the 400s covers 3:3-12:1, and a Sahidic fragment survives (Lake). The papyrus often confirms or improves the text (5:2; 9:2; 10:2). The Plain English Translation follows Lake throughout and gives the differences in the variants.

The letter claims to be by Ignatius, writing from Troas on the way to Rome (12:1), and tells of peace restored at Antioch (11:2). Eusebius knew it as his and quotes it (Church History 3.36.10-11). The saying of the risen Christ in 3:2 has an uncertain source: Eusebius did not know it, Jerome gave it to the Gospel according to the Hebrews, Origen knew it from a 'Teaching of Peter' (Lightfoot). The seven letters' genuineness was long debated, and the debate was renewed in the twentieth century: the authorship section gives the Catholic Encyclopedia's judgment of 1910, with its caveat, and the later challenges and replies.

Matches: Christ of David's line (1:1; Romans 1:3), born of a virgin (Matthew 1:23), baptized 'to fulfill all righteousness' (Matthew 3:15), crucified under Pilate and Herod (Acts 4:27), risen in the flesh and eating with the disciples (3:2-3; Luke 24:39-43; Acts 10:41); the test of confessing Christ 'come in the flesh' (5:2; 1 John 4:2); care for widows and orphans (6:2; James 1:27). Goes beyond: the rule that no thanksgiving, baptism or love feast is valid without the overseer (8:1-2) has no parallel in the New Testament, where one church can have several 'overseers' (Philippians 1:1), the elders of Ephesus are called overseers (Acts 20:17, 28), and no such rule is given; churches read this difference in different ways (see the card at chapter 8 and the cards on bishops). The saying of 3:2 is in no Gospel. Conflicts: none on a point of doctrine. On whether 'the thanksgiving is the flesh of our Savior' (7:1) agrees with each church's reading of the Gospels, see the card at Matthew 26:26.

how_to_read.b: Read 1-7 as one argument (Christ was truly human, so keep away from those who deny it) and 8-9 as its practical answer (stay with the overseer). The second half makes most sense in the light of the first.
Where the variants cite B, they give the Berlin papyrus, a copy made in the 400s (Lake). Lake often follows it.

how_to_read.h: As a witness the churches read differently
how_to_read.b: Catholic teaching quotes these chapters for the bishop and the Eucharist (Catechism 830; 1369). Churches differ on what they require today: the card at chapter 8 gives each church's rule from its own documents, and the notes point to the cards on the 66 books.
